name: IBM Cloud
tagline: Enterprise cloud platform with pay-as-you-go Virtual Servers for VPC
description: IBM Cloud offers Virtual Servers for VPC on a pay-as-you-go, per-hour billing model, plus a 30-day $200 trial credit — aimed more at developers than beginner site owners.
about: IBM Cloud is a large enterprise cloud platform covering everything from AI and data services to mainframes — this profile covers only one narrow slice of it: Virtual Servers for VPC (VSI), the Infrastructure-as-a-Service option someone could use to host a website, plus IBM's free-tier/trial terms. It is not a review of IBM Cloud's full enterprise service catalog.

Virtual Servers for VPC bill by the hour with no long-term contract required. Entry-level shared-core profiles (2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM, such as the cx2-2x4) have been tracked by third-party cloud-pricing trackers at roughly $0.06–$0.10/hour, which works out to somewhere around $45–$70/month depending on region and any commitment discount — IBM's own pricing calculator requires signing in to get a live, region-specific quote, so treat this as an approximate range rather than a fixed sticker price.

IBM Cloud does not offer a permanent free virtual server. New accounts get a $200 credit good for 30 days, and separately a Lite-plan tier that gives always-free access to 40+ other IBM Cloud services (Watson APIs, Cloud Foundry runtime memory, storage, etc.) — but there is no perpetual free VSI to run a website on indefinitely, unlike some competitors' always-free compute tiers. Anyone provisioning a VSI to host a site should expect to pay from day one after the trial credit runs out.
policies: IBM Cloud is pay-as-you-go for Virtual Servers for VPC — you're billed hourly for what you provision, with no fixed-term contract required, and no blanket money-back guarantee beyond the $200 / 30-day trial credit given to new accounts.

Standard IBM Cloud support is tied to the support plan attached to the account (Basic support is free but limited to account/billing issues; technical support requires a paid support tier). Check IBM's own support and SLA documentation before committing production workloads.
